docs.title: PhysicsNeMo ML Development
docs.text: A personal learning journal for deploying, training, and using NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo machine learning models.

docs.title: About This Project
docs.text:
This documentation tracks every step of my journey learning NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo — from setting up a development environment on Windows/WSL to training physics-informed neural networks with GPU-accelerated containers.

Whether you're starting from scratch or looking for a quick reference, this site covers the full workflow:

  • WSL2 Environment

    Set up Windows Subsystem for Linux with GPU passthrough, memory tuning, and VS Code integration for ML workloads.

    WSL Setup Guide

  • Docker & NVIDIA Runtime

    Install Docker (Engine or Desktop) and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit to run GPU-accelerated containers.

    Docker Installation

  • PhysicsNeMo Container

    Pull the official NGC container, launch interactive sessions, and mount your workspace for development.

    Container Setup

  • VS Code Dev Container

    Open the project in a fully configured development container with GPU support, debugger, and Jupyter.

    Dev Container Config

  • Remote Desktop (DCV)

    Set up NICE DCV on NVIDIA cloud VMs for a GPU-free desktop session while keeping the GPU for ML.

    DCV Setup

docs.title: Official NVIDIA Resources
docs.text: Resource Description  PhysicsNeMo Documentation Official user guide, API reference, and tutorials  PhysicsNeMo GitHub Source code, examples, and issue tracker  NGC Container Registry Pre-built Docker images with all dependencies  NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute Free and paid courses on GPU computing and AI  Deep Learning Examples Reference implementations for training and inference

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before getting started, make sure you have:

  • A machine with an NVIDIA GPU (compute capability 7.0+)
  • Windows 10/11 (build 19041+) with WSL2, or native Ubuntu 22.04/24.04
  • At least 16 GB RAM and 50 GB free disk space

Last updated: March 2026

docs.title: Docker Installation
docs.text: Docker is the core runtime for building and running containers. This guide covers two installation paths: Docker Desktop (GUI-based) and Docker Engine (CLI-only).

docs.title: Which One Should I Choose?
docs.text:
Docker Desktop Docker Engine

Best for: Windows/macOS users who want a GUI, WSL2 integration, and automatic updates.

Pros Cons Simple GUI for managing containers Heavier resource usage Built-in WSL2 backend on Windows Requires license for large organizations Automatic updates Runs as a background service Includes Docker Compose v2

Best for: Linux servers, headless machines, or users who prefer CLI-only workflows.

Pros Cons Lightweight, no GUI overhead Manual updates Full control over daemon configuration CLI-only interface Free for all use cases Requires manual setup Standard for production environments

docs.title: Docker Desktop
docs.text:
WSL2 Backend

On Windows, Docker Desktop uses WSL2 as its backend. Make sure you have WSL2 set up before proceeding.

docs.title: Install on Windows
docs.text:
1. Download the installer from Docker Desktop for Windows
  2. Run the installer and ensure "Use WSL 2 instead of Hyper-V" is checked
  3. Follow the prompts and restart when asked
  4. Open Docker Desktop and complete the initial setup

docs.title: Install on Ubuntu (with GUI)
docs.text:
# Download the .deb package
wget https://desktop.docker.com/linux/main/amd64/docker-desktop-amd64.deb

# Install
sudo apt install ./docker-desktop-amd64.deb

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
Open a terminal (or WSL2) and run:

docker --version
sudo docker run hello-world

docs.title: Supported Ubuntu Versions
docs.text: Version Codename Ubuntu 25.10 Kinetic Ubuntu 24.04 LTS Noble Ubuntu 22.04 LTS Jammy

docs.title: Uninstall Conflicting Packages
docs.text:
Remove any unofficial Docker packages that may interfere:

sudo apt remove $(dpkg --get-selections docker.io docker-compose docker-compose-v2 /
docker-doc podman-docker containerd runc | cut -f1)

docs.title: 1. Set up Docker's apt repository
docs.text:
Add Docker's official GPG key:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install ca-certificates curl
sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg \
-o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc

Add the repository to apt sources:

sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.sources <<EOF
Types: deb
URIs: https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu
Suites: $(. /etc/os-release && echo "${UBUNTU_CODENAME:-$VERSION_CODENAME}")
Components: stable
Signed-By: /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
EOF

Update the package index:

sudo apt update

docs.title: 2. Install Docker packages
docs.text:
sudo apt install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io \
  docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin

docs.title: 3. Verify Docker is running
docs.text:
sudo systemctl status docker

If the service is not active, start it:

sudo systemctl start docker

docs.title: 4. Test the installation
docs.text:
sudo docker run hello-world

You have successfully installed Docker Engine

The hello-world container downloads a test image, runs it, prints a confirmation message, and exits.

docs.title: Post-Installation Steps
docs.text: These steps apply to both Docker Desktop and Docker Engine installations.

docs.title: Manage Docker as a Non-Root User
docs.text:
Security Notice

The docker group grants root-level privileges. Only add trusted users to this group.

  1. Create the docker group:
sudo groupadd docker
  1. Add your user to the group:
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
  1. Activate the group changes:
newgrp docker
  1. Verify you can run Docker without sudo:
docker run hello-world

docs.title: Configure Docker to Start on Boot
docs.text:
Ubuntu Default

On Ubuntu, Docker starts automatically on boot. Use these commands only to change this behavior.

Enable auto-startDisable auto-start 
sudo systemctl enable docker.service
sudo systemctl enable containerd.service

sudo systemctl disable docker.service
sudo systemctl disable containerd.service

docs.title: Useful Docker Commands
docs.text: Command Description docker ps List running containers docker ps -a List all containers (including stopped) docker images List downloaded images docker system prune Remove unused data (stopped containers, dangling images) docker logs -f <name> Follow container logs docker exec -it <name> bash Open a shell in a running container

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: With Docker installed, proceed to set up the NVIDIA Container Toolkit for GPU support.

docs.title: NVIDIA Container Toolkit
docs.text: The NVIDIA Container Toolkit enables Docker containers to access the host system's NVIDIA GPUs for accelerated computing. It integrates with Docker Engine to automatically mount GPU drivers and libraries into containers at launch — no driver installation needed inside the container.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before installing the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, ensure you have:

  • Docker installed and running
  • An NVIDIA GPU with compatible drivers installed on the host
  • Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04

Check your GPU driver

Verify your host NVIDIA driver is working:

```bash
nvidia-smi
```

If this command fails, install the NVIDIA driver on your host first (or on Windows if using WSL2 — see [WSL Setup](wsl-setup.md)).

docs.title: 1. Install prerequisites
docs.text:
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
  ca-certificates \
  curl \
  gnupg2

docs.title: 2. Configure the repository
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/gpgkey | sudo gpg \
--dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg && curl \
-s -L https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/stable/deb/nvidia-container-toolkit.list | \
sed 's#deb https://#deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg] https://#g' \
| sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nvidia-container-toolkit.list

docs.title: 3. Update the package list
docs.text: sudo apt-get update

docs.title: 4. Install the toolkit
docs.text:
export NVIDIA_CONTAINER_TOOLKIT_VERSION=1.18.2-1

sudo apt-get install -y \
nvidia-container-toolkit=${NVIDIA_CONTAINER_TOOLKIT_VERSION} \
nvidia-container-toolkit-base=${NVIDIA_CONTAINER_TOOLKIT_VERSION} \
libnvidia-container-tools=${NVIDIA_CONTAINER_TOOLKIT_VERSION} \
libnvidia-container1=${NVIDIA_CONTAINER_TOOLKIT_VERSION}

Version Pinning

The this example uses 1.18.2-1. Check the NVIDIA Container Toolkit releases for the latest version.

docs.title: 1. Register the NVIDIA runtime
docs.text:
sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker

This modifies /etc/docker/daemon.json to add the NVIDIA runtime.

docs.title: 2. Restart Docker
docs.text: sudo systemctl restart docker

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
??? question "nvidia-smi works on host but not in container" - Ensure the NVIDIA runtime is configured: check /etc/docker/daemon.json for the nvidia runtime entry - Restart Docker: sudo systemctl restart docker - Use --runtime=nvidia --gpus all flags when running containers

Permission denied errors

Make sure your user is in the docker group (see Docker post-install).

Toolkit version conflicts

Remove all existing toolkit packages and reinstall:

```bash
sudo apt-get remove nvidia-container-toolkit*
sudo apt-get install nvidia-container-toolkit
```

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• NVIDIA Container Toolkit Documentation
  • NVIDIA Container Toolkit GitHub

docs.title: WSL2 Setup for ML Development
docs.text:
This guide walks through setting up Windows Subsystem for Linux 2 (WSL2) as a development environment for GPU-accelerated machine learning workflows.

Setup for windows only

This guide is specific to windows and can be skipped if you are using Ubuntu.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Windows Version Requirements

  • Windows 10 version 2004 (build 19041) or later
  • Windows 11 — any version
  • BIOS/UEFI virtualization must be enabled (Intel VT-x or AMD-V)

NVIDIA GPU Driver

You must install the Windows-side NVIDIA GPU driver (not the Linux one). WSL2 uses GPU paravirtualization, so the Windows driver handles GPU communication. Download the latest driver from NVIDIA Driver Downloads.

docs.title: Enable and Install WSL
docs.text:
Open PowerShell as Administrator and run:

wsl --install

This command enables the required features and installs Ubuntu as the default distribution. Restart your machine when prompted.

Choosing a Different Distribution

To see available distributions:

wsl --list --online

To install a specific one (e.g., Ubuntu 24.04):

wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04

docs.title: Verify WSL2 is Active
docs.text:
After restarting, confirm WSL2 is being used:

wsl --list --verbose

Expected output:

  NAME            STATE           VERSION
* Ubuntu          Running         2

docs.title: Memory and CPU Limits (.wslconfig)
docs.text:
By default, WSL2 can use up to 50% of your system RAM and all CPU cores. For ML workloads you'll want to tune this to balance between WSL and Windows.

Create or edit %USERPROFILE%\.wslconfig (e.g., C:\Users\YourName\.wslconfig):

[wsl2]
memory=24GB
processors=28
swap=4GB
localhostForwarding=true

[experimental]
autoMemoryReclaim=gradual
sparseVhd=true

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Maximum RAM that WSL2 can use. Leave at least 4–6 GB for Windows to avoid system slowdowns.

Total System RAM Recommended WSL2 memory 16 GB 10–12 GB 32 GB 24–28 GB 64 GB 48–56 GB

docs.title: Processors
docs.text:
Number of logical CPU cores to allocate to WSL2. To check how many you have, run in PowerShell:

(Get-CimInstance Win32_Processor).NumberOfLogicalProcessors

Rule of thumb: Leave 2–4 cores for Windows and give the rest to WSL2. For example, on a 16-core machine, set processors=12.

docs.title: Swap
docs.text:
Swap acts as a safety net — if your training job temporarily exceeds the memory limit, it spills to disk instead of being killed immediately (OOM). Setting swap=0 disables this safety net entirely.

Don't disable swap for ML workloads

While you never want training to run on swap (it would be very slow), having a small swap buffer (2–4 GB) prevents your long-running training job from being killed if it briefly exceeds the memory limit. Think of it as insurance, not working memory.

docs.title: LocalhostForwarding
docs.text: When set to true, any service running inside WSL2 (e.g., Jupyter on port 8888, TensorBoard on 6006) is automatically accessible from Windows at localhost:<port>. Without this, you'd need to find WSL2's internal virtual IP (hostname -I inside WSL) and use that address instead, which changes every time WSL restarts.

docs.title: AutoMemoryReclaim
docs.text: Set to gradual so WSL2 gradually returns unused memory to Windows over time. Without this, WSL2 holds onto all memory it has ever used, even after processes finish.

docs.title: SparseVhd
docs.text:
WSL2 stores its entire Linux filesystem in a single virtual hard disk file (.vhdx). By default, this file only grows — if you download 10 GB of data and then delete it, the .vhdx file remains 10 GB on your Windows drive.

With sparseVhd=true, the .vhdx file automatically shrinks when space is freed inside WSL, so it only uses the actual disk space needed.

Applying Changes

After editing .wslconfig, restart WSL2:

wsl --shutdown

Then reopen your Ubuntu terminal.

docs.title: Verify GPU Access
docs.text:
WSL2 supports GPU passthrough natively with the Windows NVIDIA driver. Inside your WSL2 terminal:

nvidia-smi

You should see your GPU listed. If not, ensure:

  1. You installed the Windows NVIDIA driver (not a Linux one inside WSL)
  2. Your Windows build is recent enough
  3. WSL2 is fully updated: wsl --update from PowerShell

docs.title: CUDA inside WSL2
docs.text:
The NVIDIA driver provides CUDA support automatically via /usr/lib/wsl/lib/. You do not need to install CUDA inside WSL — Docker containers bring their own CUDA runtime.

Do NOT Install Linux NVIDIA Drivers

Installing nvidia-driver-* packages inside WSL2 will conflict with the Windows driver passthrough and break GPU access. Only install the driver on the Windows side.

docs.title: VS Code Remote — WSL Integration
docs.text:
Do NOT open WSL paths directly from Windows

Opening VS Code on Windows and navigating to a \\wsl$\Ubuntu\... path does not use the WSL extension. VS Code will run entirely on the Windows side, accessing Linux files over the network — this makes file operations, IntelliSense, and builds significantly slower. Always connect to WSL using one of the methods below.

docs.title: Clone the Repository inside WSL
docs.text:
Open your WSL terminal (Ubuntu) and clone the project into the Linux filesystem:

# cd to the desired clone location
git clone <repository-url>

Always store projects on the Linux filesystem

Keep your code under /home/<user>/ inside WSL — not on /mnt/c/ or any Windows mount. Cross-filesystem access is significantly slower.

docs.title: Connect VS Code to WSL
docs.text:
1. Open VS Code on Windows normally
  2. Press Ctrl+Shift+P to open the Command Palette
  3. Type WSL: Connect to WSL and select it — VS Code will reload connected to your WSL instance
  4. Once connected (you'll see WSL: Ubuntu in the bottom-left corner), use File → Open Folder and navigate to your project:

Open Folder directly in WSL

You can also use WSL: Open Folder in WSL... from the Command Palette to connect and open a folder in a single step.

docs.title: Recommended Extensions
docs.text:
Install these extensions inside the WSL session (they need to run on the Linux side):

Extension Purpose Dev Containers Open projects inside Docker containers Container Tools Container management from the sidebar

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
GPU not detected in WSL2 
1. Ensure the **Windows** NVIDIA driver is up to date
  1. Run wsl --update from PowerShell
  2. Restart WSL: wsl --shutdown
  3. Verify with nvidia-smi inside WSL
Out of memory errors during training

Increase the memory value in .wslconfig and restart WSL. Also check that swap is configured.

Slow filesystem performance

Store your ML projects on the Linux filesystem (/home/user/), not on Windows mounts (/mnt/c/). Cross-filesystem access is significantly slower.

docs.title: PhysicsNeMo Container Setup
docs.text: NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo is an open-source framework for developing physics-informed machine learning models that blend physical laws with observational data. It enables the creation of high-speed AI surrogates to simulate complex engineering problems thousands of times faster than traditional numerical solvers.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before pulling the container, ensure you have:

  • Docker installed
  • NVIDIA Container Toolkit configured

docs.title: Pull the Container
docs.text:
Download the PhysicsNeMo Docker container from NGC:

docker pull nvcr.io/nvidia/physicsnemo/physicsnemo:<tag>

Available Tags

Browse all available tags on the PhysicsNeMo NGC Container page.

As of this writing, the latest tag is `25.11`.

docs.title: Launching Container Sessions
docs.text:
Replace <tag>

In all commands below, replace <tag> with your installed version (e.g., 25.11).

docs.title: Basic Shell Session
docs.text:
Start an interactive shell with GPU access:

docker run \
  --shm-size=1g \
  --ulimit memlock=-1 \
  --ulimit stack=67108864 \
  --runtime nvidia \
  -it --rm \
  nvcr.io/nvidia/physicsnemo/physicsnemo:<tag> bash

docs.title: Shell Session with Workspace Mounted
docs.text:
Mount your current directory into the container for accessing your project files:

docker run \
  --shm-size=1g \
  --ulimit memlock=-1 \
  --ulimit stack=67108864 \
  --runtime nvidia \
  -v ${PWD}:/workspace \
  -it --rm \
  nvcr.io/nvidia/physicsnemo/physicsnemo:<tag> bash

Mounting Directories

The -v ${PWD}:/workspace flag mounts your current directory to /workspace inside the container. Changes to files in /workspace persist on your host machine.

docs.title: Session with Jupyter Lab
docs.text:
Launch a Jupyter Lab server accessible from your browser:

docker run \
  --shm-size=1g \
  --ulimit memlock=-1 \
  --ulimit stack=67108864 \
  --runtime nvidia \
  -v ${PWD}:/workspace \
  -p 8888:8888 \
  -it --rm \
  nvcr.io/nvidia/physicsnemo/physicsnemo:<tag> \
  jupyter lab --ip=0.0.0.0 --no-browser --allow-root

Then open http://localhost:8888 in your browser and paste the token from the terminal output.

docs.title: Understanding the Docker Run Flags
docs.text: Flag Purpose --shm-size=1g Sets shared memory size — increase for multi-process data loading --ulimit memlock=-1 Removes memory locking limits (required for GPU pinned memory) --ulimit stack=67108864 Sets stack size to 64MB (required by some CUDA operations) --runtime nvidia Uses the NVIDIA container runtime for GPU access --gpus all Exposes all GPUs to the container -v host:container Bind-mounts a host directory into the container -p host:container Maps a container port to the host (e.g., for Jupyter) -it Interactive mode with a pseudo-TTY --rm Automatically remove the container when it exits

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Set up a VS Code Dev Container for a fully integrated development experience
  • Explore the PhysicsNeMo documentation for tutorials and API reference
  • Check out example models on GitHub

docs.title: VS Code Dev Container
docs.text: This project includes a pre-configured Dev Container that launches the PhysicsNeMo NGC container directly in VS Code with GPU support, debugging tools, and Jupyter integration.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Docker installed and running
  • NVIDIA Container Toolkit configured
  • VS Code with the Dev Containers extension

docs.title: Open in Dev Container
docs.text:
1. Open the project folder in VS Code
  2. Press Ctrl+Shift+P and select Dev Containers: Reopen in Container
  3. VS Code will pull the PhysicsNeMo image (if needed) and launch the container
  4. Wait for the post-creation setup to complete (installs pip and jupyter)

First Launch

The first time you open the Dev Container, it needs to pull the ~15 GB PhysicsNeMo image. Subsequent launches are much faster since the image is cached locally.

docs.title: Configuration Explained
docs.text: The Dev Container is defined in .devcontainer/devcontainer.json. Here's what each section does:

docs.title: Container Image
docs.text:
"image": "nvcr.io/nvidia/physicsnemo/physicsnemo:25.11"

Uses the official PhysicsNeMo container from NVIDIA NGC. Change the tag to use a different version.

docs.title: GPU and Runtime Arguments
docs.text:
"runArgs": [
    "--gpus=all",
    "--shm-size=8g",
    "--ulimit", "memlock=-1",
    "--ulimit", "stack=67108864",
    "--runtime=nvidia"
]
Argument Purpose --gpus=all Exposes all NVIDIA GPUs to the container --shm-size=8g 8 GB shared memory for multi-worker data loading --ulimit memlock=-1 Unlimited memory locking (required by CUDA) --ulimit stack=67108864 64 MB stack size (required by some CUDA ops) --runtime=nvidia Enables the NVIDIA container runtime

docs.title: Workspace Mount
docs.text:
"workspaceMount": "source=${localWorkspaceFolder},target=/workspace,type=bind,consistency=cached",
"workspaceFolder": "/workspace"

Mounts your local project folder to /workspace inside the container. The cached consistency mode improves filesystem performance on macOS/WSL2.

docs.title: Port Forwarding
docs.text:
"forwardPorts": [8888],
"portsAttributes": {
    "8888": {
        "label": "Jupyter",
        "onAutoForward": "notify"
    }
}

Automatically forwards port 8888 for Jupyter Lab. VS Code will notify you when the port becomes available.

docs.title: Post-Creation Command
docs.text:
"postCreateCommand": "pip install --upgrade pip jupyter"

Runs after the container is created to ensure pip and jupyter are up to date.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
The Dev Container automatically installs these VS Code extensions inside the container:

Extension Purpose Remote Containers Container management Docker Docker sidebar integration GitHub Copilot + Chat AI code assistance Jupyter (suite) Notebook editing, rendering, cell tags Python + Pylance Python language support and IntelliSense Python Debugger (debugpy) Interactive debugging Python Environments Virtual environment management YAML YAML file editing

docs.title: Adding Python Packages
docs.text:
To install additional packages that persist across container rebuilds, modify the postCreateCommand:

"postCreateCommand": "pip install --upgrade pip jupyter tensorboard wandb"

docs.title: Changing the PhysicsNeMo Version
docs.text:
Update the image field with a different tag from the NGC Container Registry:

"image": "nvcr.io/nvidia/physicsnemo/physicsnemo:<new-tag>"

Then rebuild the container: Ctrl+Shift+P → Dev Containers: Rebuild Container.

docs.title: Adding More Port Forwards
docs.text:
To expose additional services (e.g., TensorBoard on port 6006):

"forwardPorts": [8888, 6006],
"portsAttributes": {
    "8888": { "label": "Jupyter", "onAutoForward": "notify" },
    "6006": { "label": "TensorBoard", "onAutoForward": "notify" }
}

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Container fails to start with GPU errors

Ensure the NVIDIA Container Toolkit is properly configured and Docker can access the GPU:

docker run --rm --runtime=nvidia --gpus all ubuntu nvidia-smi
Extensions not installing

Rebuild the container: Ctrl+Shift+P → Dev Containers: Rebuild Container

Slow filesystem performance

If using WSL2, ensure your project files are on the Linux filesystem (/home/user/), not on a Windows mount (/mnt/c/).

docs.title: DCV Remote Desktop for NVIDIA VMs
docs.text:
NVIDIA Optimized VMI

This section is only for cloud VM Linux installations. Refer to the NVIDIA Optimized VMI documentation.

This setup gives you a lightweight desktop (for VS Code, browsers, and debugging).

docs.title: System Preparation
docs.text: NVIDIA Optimized VMI does not include a desktop environment. You need to install one.

docs.title: 1. Update and Install Minimal Desktop
docs.text:
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt install -y ubuntu-desktop-minimal

WIP
